THOUGHT: This 40-year-old nulliparous woman presents with subacute onset of shortness of breath and increasing abdominal girth over one month. Physical exam reveals signs of right-sided pleural effusion (dullness, decreased breath sounds), ascites (shifting dullness, fluid wave), and a right pelvic mass. Imaging confirms a large right ovarian mass and ascites, and chest X-ray shows a right pleural effusion. The triad of ovarian mass + ascites + pleural effusion is highly characteristic of Meigs syndrome — a benign condition classically defined as the triad of a benign ovarian tumor (most commonly fibroma, but also thecoma, granulosa cell tumor, or Brenner tumor), ascites, and pleural effusion. Although CA-125 is often elevated in ovarian malignancy, it can be normal in Meigs syndrome — and its normal level here further argues against malignancy. The absence of weight loss, night sweats, fever, or constitutional symptoms, along with normal CBC and lack of other red flags (e.g., bowel/urinary changes, leg swelling), makes malignant ovarian cancer less likely. While primary peritoneal carcinoma or advanced ovarian cancer could present similarly, they almost invariably elevate CA-125 and are associated with more systemic symptoms — neither of which is present. Nulliparity is a risk factor for ovarian tumors but does not favor malignancy per se. The benign nature of the syndrome is confirmed histologically post-resection, but clinically, Meigs syndrome is the most appropriate diagnosis given the classic triad and absence of malignant features.

DIAGNOSIS: Meigs syndrome
